elements.evidence: "Customer may terminate this Agreement for convenience"
"upon 30 days' prior written notice to Commerce One"
"shall refund to Customer any prepaid fees on a pro-rata basis for the period after the effective date of termination"

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during any committed term."
"upon 30 days' prior written notice" (shorter than 60–90 days; preferred bargain instead)

elements.element: Early-termination fee not exceeding 3 months' fees
elements.evidence: No early-termination fee mechanic appears in 11.1A

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at end of a term on 90 days' notice
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during any committed term." (absolute prohibition during committed term, no end-of-term 90-day right)

offending_extra_words: Corio is the Customer under this Agreement.
reasons: The inserted 11.1A completes every atomic element of the preferred position: Customer convenience right, 30 days' prior written notice, pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, and an express bar on Vendor (Commerce One) convenience termination during a committed term.

The fallback bargain is not met on its own terms (30 days rather than 60–90 days, no early-termination fee cap, no end-of-term Vendor right), but that is irrelevant because the locked preferred level is satisfied.

Minimality is short of clean: the agreement's defined party is "Corio", so the added definitional sentence "Corio is the Customer under this Agreement." is unnecessary boilerplate — drafting the clause with "Corio" directly would have avoided introducing a new alias while achieving the same effect.
No unrelated commercial term is disturbed: 11.1 term/renewal and 11.2 cause and insolvency termination remain fully effective, and no contradiction or dangling mechanic is created.
